headline: Local teen smashes soapbox derby record
standfirst: Heaviest cart in the field wins, and straw bales save the day
brief: The sports desk filed this in a hurry. The story is good, but the physics needs checking before it runs.

body.t: Fifteen-year-old Priya Nair stormed to victory at Saturday's Ridgeway Soapbox Derby, rolling her home-built cart down the 400-metre course in just 40 seconds.
That is an average speed of 10 metres per second, the fastest in the event's history.
body.ok: It is correct: average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 metres per second.

body.t: Her cart was the heaviest in the race, and because gravity makes heavier objects accelerate faster, she pulled away from the lighter carts at the start.

options: Gravity does not act on a cart once it is rolling.
Gravity alone gives every mass the same acceleration: a larger weight is matched by a larger mass.
Heavier objects accelerate more slowly, because the same gravitational pull has more mass to get moving, so the lightest carts should lead.
feedback: Gravity acts on the cart for the whole race: its weight is what drives it down the hill.
This is the opposite mistake. Without resistive forces, mass makes no difference to the acceleration.
err.fix: Her cart was the heaviest in the race; gravity alone would give every cart the same acceleration on the same slope, but resistive forces slow a heavier cart less, so she pulled away from the lighter carts.
keys: Acceleration due to gravity alone does not depend on mass.
Any advantage of the extra mass comes from resistive forces having less effect.

body.t: Organisers clocked her at 17 metres per second at the finish line, well above her average because she had been speeding up for most of the race.
body.ok: It is correct: a cart that speeds up during the race finishes faster than its average speed.

body.t: Nair credits her success to a set of carefully polished axles, which she says let the force of motion inside the cart keep it going.

options: No force is needed to keep an object moving, and a “force of motion” does not exist.
Polished axles increase friction, so they could not help.
The force of motion only exists while the cart is speeding up, and once the cart reaches a steady speed it fades away.
feedback: Polishing an axle reduces friction, so this part of the story is fine. The problem is the idea of what keeps the cart moving.
A force is always exerted by one object on another. A moving object has momentum and kinetic energy, but no force “inside” it.
err.fix: Nair credits her success to a set of carefully polished axles, which reduce friction, so there is less resistive force to slow the cart down.
keys: No force is needed to maintain motion (Newton's first law).
The axles help by reducing the resistive force.

body.t: With less friction at the axles, less of the cart's gravitational potential energy was transferred to thermal energy on the way down.
body.ok: It is correct: friction transfers mechanical energy to thermal energy, so less friction means less energy transferred this way.

body.t: On the final straight the cart settled at a steady top speed, the moment when the resultant force on it was at its greatest.

options: At a steady top speed the resultant force on the cart is at its smallest but not zero, because it is still moving.
A steady top speed needs a constant resultant force in the direction of motion.
At a steady speed in a straight line the acceleration is zero, so the resultant force is zero.
feedback: If there were any resultant force, the cart would still be accelerating. Being in motion does not need a resultant force.
A constant resultant force gives a constant acceleration, not a constant speed.
err.fix: On the final straight the cart settled at a steady top speed, the moment when the forces on it balanced and the resultant force was zero.
keys: So the resultant force is zero (the forces balance).

body.t: Stopping safely took a 20-metre run-off lane lined with straw bales.
The bales absorb the cart's momentum, so that its change in momentum is much smaller than it would be if it hit a wall.

options: The change in momentum is actually larger with bales, because they keep pushing back on the cart for a longer time.
The change in momentum is the same either way; the longer stop means a smaller average force.
Momentum is not involved in stopping: only energy is.
feedback: From the same speed to rest is the same change in momentum, whatever stops the cart.
Stopping a moving cart is a change in momentum, and the force on it equals the rate of that change.
err.fix: The bales make the cart take longer to stop; its change in momentum is the same as if it stopped dead against a wall, so the rate of change of momentum, and the average force, is much smaller.
keys: The change in momentum is the same.
A longer stopping time means a smaller average force.

body.t: Nair's helmet protects her in a similar way, because its foam crushes and lengthens the time of any impact on her head.
body.ok: It is correct: a crushable helmet increases the time over which the head's momentum changes, reducing the average force.

body.t: Race officials warn that if next year's carts go twice as fast, each one will have twice as much kinetic energy to get rid of in the run-off lane.

options: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed, so doubling the speed gives four times the kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy depends only on mass, so it would not change.
Doubling the speed halves the kinetic energy, because the cart spends less time on the track.
feedback: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed: $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
The time on the track has no effect on the kinetic energy at the finish. Look at how $E_\text{k}$ depends on $v$.
err.fix: Race officials warn that if next year's carts go twice as fast, each one will have four times as much kinetic energy to get rid of in the run-off lane.
keys: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Doubling the speed gives four times the kinetic energy.

body.t: Nair is already working on a more streamlined body for next year, which should reduce the air resistance on the cart at high speed.
body.ok: It is correct: streamlining reduces drag, and drag matters most at high speed.
